_**Tribes: Vengeance**_ is a [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction")[first-person shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_shooter "First-person shooter") video game developed by [Irrational Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrational_Games "Irrational Games") and released by [Vivendi Universal Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivendi_Universal_Games "Vivendi Universal Games") in October 2004. It was built on an enhanced version of the [Unreal Engine 2.5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unreal_Engine_2.5 "Unreal Engine 2.5"), which Irrational Games called the Vengeance engine. Part of the [_Tribes_ series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribes_(video_game_series) "Tribes (video game series)"), in addition to its multiplayer network maps, _Vengeance_ includes a complete single-player campaign.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tribes:_Vengeance&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

As a primarily [first-person shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_shooter "First-person shooter"), _Tribes: Vengeance_ places the player in control of an infantry soldier in [power armor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_armor "Power armor"). While the game is tailored for first-person shooting, the player can also toggle to a third-person view at any time. Additionally, there are multiple pilotable vehicles, which are restricted to third-person camera.

The game's most distinguishing features are the jetpacks and "skis" offered on all variants of the power armor. Jetpacks allow the player to fly for short periods of time, using the player's energy meter. This energy regenerates whenever the jetpack is not active. Skiing may be activated any time the player is on foot and does not cost energy; this switches the player to a frictionless ground-travel mode, allowing the player to slide very rapidly down slopes and (with sufficient speed before activating the skis) across flat terrain. Skiing up a slope will cause the player to slow due to gravity.

Combat occurs primarily with ranged weapons, including bullet and explosive projectile firearms. Each character, vehicle, and machine has [hit points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_points "Hit points"). Anything with hit points may be repaired by "repair packs"; infantry may also pick up medkits dropped by other infantry upon death. The game offers three classes of armor: light, medium, and heavy. Heavier armor offers more hit points and ammunition but slower movement.

The player has three weapon slots, grenades, and a utility slot; the utility slot holds items such as repair packs, speed packs, energy packs and deployables like repair stations, turrets and inventory stations.

The introduction of a grappler gun adds another aspect to movement in the game. This is the first and only game in the Tribes franchise to include such a mechanic.

### Single-player

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tribes:_Vengeance&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Single-player")]

The single player campaign follows five playable characters (Victoria, Daniel, Julia, Mercury, and Jericho) whom the player navigates through 18 missions. The missions are played in [achronological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_(arts) "Nonlinear (arts)") order, set either in "The Past" (Victoria, Daniel, Julia, Mercury) or in "The Present" (Julia, Jericho, Mercury), with the former detailing the story of Julia's birth and childhood and the latter describing her search for vengeance upon the Tribals and later, for her own [psychological identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_identity "Psychological identity").

### Multiplayer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tribes:_Vengeance&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Multiplayer")]

The multiplayer mode offers five different default game types and a diversity of map locations. Players are ranked during matches by points they acquire through the match. You can get offensive (killing an opponent, capturing a flag, or destroying enemy equipment), defensive (returning a flag, repairing your equipment, or killing an enemy flag carrier), or by style points (hit a head shot with a sniper rifle, or hitting someone in mid-air with a spinfusor disk).

*   **Arena** is a 'Team Free for All' in which two teams fight for up to 9 rounds. There is no [respawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respawn "Respawn"), so once a player dies, they must wait for the next round before they can play again. Whichever team has more rounds won at the end of a match wins. This game type is inherited from earlier _[Tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribes\_(video\_game) "Tribes (video game)")_ games.
*   **Ball** is a game type where two teams play against each other with a goal for each team. There is a single ball located somewhere on the map, usually in the middle. The objective is to get the ball and throw it into the enemy's goal. Whichever team has the most points at the end wins. This game is original to _Tribes: Vengeance_, but also resembles [Unreal Tournament 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unreal_Tournament_2003 "Unreal Tournament 2003") and [Unreal Tournament 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unreal_Tournament_2004 "Unreal Tournament 2004")'s [Bombing Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_Run?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bombing Run (page does not exist)") game.

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/85/Tv_emerald-1.jpg/250px-Tv_emerald-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tv_emerald-1.jpg)

Maps can differ from a lush terrain like this to a rough desert landscape.

*   In **Fuel**, both teams have a fuel depot at their base. There is one neutral fuel depot which the players can collect fuel from, as well as a depot for each team. Players may stand within these to gradually steal fuel or, if it is their own team's, to deposit fuel. The less fuel in the depot, the slower it takes to collect it. As well as the depots, players can collect fuel cells from the ground that may have originally spawned there randomly on the game's start, or have been dropped upon a player's death. The maximum amount of fuel a character can carry is 15, and each fuel cell contains a specific amount of fuel. Whenever a player dies, their team's fuel depot loses one unit of fuel. Whichever team fills their depot first is the winner. This game type is original to _Tribes: Vengeance_
*   **Rabbit** is the only 'Free for All' game mode in _Tribes: Vengeance_. In this, there are no teams, but a single flag on the map somewhere, usually in the middle of the map. The objective for every player is to retrieve the flag and run. Whenever a player retrieves the flag, every other player will be alerted, and whoever has the flag will be marked as their enemy. Points are gained by holding on to the flag as long as possible and killing the other players. Points are lost by killing somebody who does not have the flag. No points are gained by killing the flag carrier. The game is timed, and whoever has the most points at the end is the winner. This game mode is common to all _Tribes_ games, as well as many other games.
*   **[Capture the Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_the_Flag "Capture the Flag")** mode is similar to its _Tribes_ equivalent. There are two teams, each with a flag and a flag stand. The objective for each team is to capture the enemy flag and bring it back to their base. However, the team's flag must be at their flag stand in order for them to capture the enemy's flag. _**The Getaway**_ is an [action-adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action-adventure "Action-adventure") video game developed by [Team Soho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Soho "Team Soho") and published by [Sony Computer Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Computer_Entertainment "Sony Computer Entertainment") for the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"). It was released on 11 December 2002. It is inspired by British [gangster films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangster_film "Gangster film") such as _[Get Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get\_Carter "Get Carter")_ (1971) and _[Snatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snatch\_(film) "Snatch (film)")_ (2000).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-SonyUS-2) The game was planned to be released alongside the launch of the PlayStation 2 in 2000, but was delayed by over two years due to the difficulty of recreating large areas of [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") in [high resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_resolution "Image resolution").

_The Getaway_ focuses on two characters: Mark Hammond, an ex-bank robber, and Frank Carter, a police officer in service with the [Flying Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Squad "Flying Squad"). Both plots run parallel and intersect before concluding in the finale of the game. A sequel, _[The Getaway: Black Monday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Getaway:\_Black\_Monday "The Getaway: Black Monday")_, was released in 2004. A spin-off, _[Gangs of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangs\_of\_London\_(video\_game) "Gangs of London (video game)")_, was released in 2006; this spawned the 2020 [television adaptation of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangs_of_London_(TV_series) "Gangs of London (TV series)") and a 2022 graphic novel.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

_The Getaway_ is an [action-adventure game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action-adventure_game "Action-adventure game") played from [third-person view](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-person_view "Third-person view") in which the player controls the two lead characters in an [open world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") as they carry out their missions for game progression. Both of the characters can perform a series of physical tasks such as walking, sprinting, rolling, shooting, and taking cover during a gunfight. Once Mark Hammond's missions are completed, free-roaming is unlocked for his character,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer-3) which allows the player to roam around the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London") and [Central London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_London "Central London") without mission objectives or time limits. Due to similarities to the _[Grand Theft Auto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Theft\_Auto "Grand Theft Auto")_ series, it is often labeled as a [_Grand Theft Auto_ clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_clone "Grand Theft Auto clone").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-6)

Unlike the _Grand Theft Auto_ series and other similar franchises, the game features a number of real vehicles that were licensed from automobile manufacturers such as [Rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MG_Rover_Group "MG Rover Group"), [Jensen Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jensen_Motors "Jensen Motors"), [Saab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saab_Automobile "Saab Automobile"), [Peugeot Citroën](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peugeot_Citro%C3%ABn "Peugeot Citroën"), [TVR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVR "TVR"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-E3_IGN-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-8)[Fiat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat "Fiat"), and [Lexus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexus "Lexus"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer-3) among others. Firearms are also based on the real world such as [Glock 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glock_17 "Glock 17") pistol, [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") assault rifle, [Remington 870](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remington_870 "Remington 870") pump-action shotgun, and [Heckler & Koch MP5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heckler_&_Koch_MP5 "Heckler & Koch MP5") submachine gun; other weapons include a meat cleaver and crowbar, among others.

A major feature of the game is its approach to being "movie-like" and immersive, which was achieved by excluding features that are present in most games; there is no [HUD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heads-up_display_(video_games) "Heads-up display (video games)") or map system: players driving in a car are guided to a destination by the car's indicators and hazard lights blinking. Running out of ammunition is signaled by the character dropping their weapon, as there isn't a health meter. Player health is regenerated by resting against a wall.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer-3)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Plot")]

The game takes place in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") during a single day, and is played through the perspectives of two characters: ex-gangster Mark Hammond and [Metropolitan Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police "Metropolitan Police") officer Frank Carter of the [Flying Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Squad "Flying Squad") unit.

### Mark Hammond

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mark Hammond")]

Mark Hammond, a former member of the [Soho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soho,_London "Soho, London")-based Collins Gang, witnesses the kidnapping of his son Alex and the murder of his wife Susie by kidnappers belonging to [Bethnal Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethnal_Green,_London "Bethnal Green, London") mob. He pursues the kidnappers to their hideout, where he is captured by their leader, Charlie Jolson. Charlie forces Mark to do his bidding by sending him to attack his former mates in the Collins gang at their Soho headquarters, ambush a prison transport van to free Charlie's nephew "Crazy" Jake Jolson, and instigate a gang war between the [Yardies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_posse "Jamaican posse") and [Triads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triad_(organized_crime) "Triad (organized crime)") by attacking their strongholds in [Chinatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown,_London "Chinatown, London") and North London. He then sends Mark to infiltrate the [Snow Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_Hill,_London "Snow Hill, London") police station to murder corrupt [Detective Chief Inspector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Inspector "Chief Inspector") Clive McCormack who is working for Charlie, and Yasmin, a freelance assassin that Jolson had hired to kidnap Alex. Whilst he kills McCormack, Mark spares Yasmin who offers to help him help find Alex in exchange. Hoping to turn the tables on Charlie, Mark steals £300,000 of Yardie drug money that he was to give to him, and attempts to trick the Jolson's into getting Alex back, while Yasmin infiltrates Charlie's mansion in [Mayfair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfair "Mayfair") posing as his girlfriend. The plan fails and both are captured by Charlie who later reveals that kidnapping Alex and using Mark is part of an ultimate plan to wipe out his rivals and take over London in their absence, with Mark acting as the scapegoat. Detective Frank Carter frees the both of them, and they make they way back to Charlie's mansion to find Alex, only to witness them taking him to a container ship, the _Sol Vita_ at [St Saviour's Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Saviour's_Dock "St Saviour's Dock"), where they confront Jolson and all of the gangs he had antagonised.

### Frank Carter

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Frank Carter")]

Detectives Frank Carter and Joe Fielding identify and arrest Jake Jolson at a brothel, though Joe is wounded during the raid. Frank follows up on the chaos instigated by Mark across London, before he is placed on escort duty when Jake is moved. Arriving too late to prevent Jake's escape, Frank is suspended by McCormack. Frank, having already been suspicious of McCormack, follows him to one of Charlie's depots. He discovers a hoard of seized evidence being repatriated to the Jolsons. Before Frank can clear his name, Mark kills McCormack. Frank visits the hospital where Joe is recovering, and saves him from a hit squad sent by the Jolson's. Joe points him in the direction of another one of Charlie's warehouses, where he finds the captured Mark and Yasmin. Left with no other options for assistance, Frank frees Mark and Yasmin and convinces them to team up with him and bring the Jolsons down. Frank learns of the meeting between Jolson and the gang aboard the ship at St. Saviour's dock and confronts them all there.

### Finale

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Finale")]

Mark, Yasmin, and Frank converge on the Sol Vita, where Charlie has taken Alex, and where he intends to wipe out the rival gangs with a bomb. Mark, Yasmin, Frank, and the gangs kill off the rest of the Bethnal Green mob and capture Charlie where they learn the truth of his plan and how he blackmailed Mark. The gangs agree to let Alex, Mark, and Yasmin go and leave London, but not Frank. Charlie, in a fit of madness, detonates the bomb. Alex, Frank, Mark and Yasmin are able to escape the ship just as bomb explodes, destroying the ship.

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Development")]

_The Getaway_'s development originated at Sony Computer Entertainment Europe on the [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console) "PlayStation (console)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-E3_IGN-7) off the back of _[Porsche Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porsche\_Challenge "Porsche Challenge")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-blog.eu.playstation.com-9) After _Porsche Challenge_, director Brendan McNamara felt that a free-roaming vehicle game was an interesting concept worth exploring. The title was prototyped and playable missions were made; several screenshots appeared in the _[Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official\_U.S.\_PlayStation\_Magazine "Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine")_. The project evolved into a [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2") game.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-E3_IGN-7) The original code was kept and there was a discussion of including it on the finished version of _The Getaway_, which would ultimately not happen. The original version has not been released.

[Bizarre Creations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizarre_Creations "Bizarre Creations") received attention due to their successful result in reproducing the streets of central London for their [Sega Dreamcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Dreamcast "Sega Dreamcast") racer _[Metropolis Street Racer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis\_Street\_Racer "Metropolis Street Racer")_ (_MSR_). As _MSR_ was being hyped and primed for release as one of the Dreamcast's so-called "[killer applications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killer_application "Killer application")", Sony Computer Entertainment Europe felt compelled to attempt to steal [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega")'s thunder by promising the creation of a PlayStation 2 title which would re-create a massive 113 square kilometers (70 square miles) of London, displaying the ferocity with which Sony Computer Entertainment Europe was willing to attempt to challenge its veteran competitor. In moving over to vastly more capable hardware, the scope of the title expanded, as did its ambitions; the unit at Sony was formally spun off as an independent unit named Team Soho. The final creation actually only yielded an area of 16 square kilometers (10 square miles).

Re-creating 16 square kilometers proved a daunting task and a technical nightmare, factors which may have delayed the release of _The Getaway_ by several years. In the case of the latter, the programmers had to perfect an engine that could constantly stream three-dimensional geometry and texture data;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-blog.eu.playstation.com-9) of the areas of London the player was in close proximity to. At no point was the city loaded into memory, as it simply would not fit. Unlike [Rockstar Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockstar_Games "Rockstar Games")'s _[Grand Theft Auto III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Theft\_Auto\_III "Grand Theft Auto III")_, it was not an acceptable option for the Team Soho developers to break the city up into separate regions and impose a loading time delay when crossing between areas.

The hype surrounding the project began in earnest just before [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3 "E3") 2000, when a series of screenshots were published online. They revealed a level of detail, showing the identifiable streets near Team Soho's studio. Though it has been argued[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] that these shots were actually mock-up pre-renders, it is possible they were taken from actual code that received further detailed vehicle and character models, higher resolution textures and also anti-aliased the final output.

Although the prototype game was shown behind closed doors, the public was not privy to its results for at least another year. It was made playable at E3 2002.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-10) By then, the project had ballooned, exceeding its development budget many times over. Sony Computer Entertainment Europe had a range of other titles in development; however, the decision was taken by [Phil Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Harrison "Phil Harrison") to can many of them, perhaps to allow yet more funds to be poured into _The Getaway_. As a result of this, the axe was to fall on two of its studios, Sony Computer Entertainment Europe Manchester and Sony Computer Entertainment Europe Leeds.

When the game was launched in December 2002 it was a huge seller across Europe, especially in the United Kingdom. Worldwide and particularly in the United States, the game received mixed reviews and sales. The fact that it was released around the same time as the hugely-popular _[Grand Theft Auto: Vice City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Theft\_Auto:\_Vice\_City "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City")_ (to which the game was often compared) also hurt sales, despite a large marketing campaign in the United States. _The Getaway_ had a marketing budget of $10.3 million.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-11) It cost £5 million to produce.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-12)

### Soundtrack

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Soundtrack")]

The game's soundtrack is complemented by a title song and cutscene soundtrack, performed by the [London Philharmonic Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Philharmonic_Orchestra "London Philharmonic Orchestra"). The game's soundtrack was chiefly composed by Andrew Hale, while portions of the soundtrack were written by [Shawn Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawn_Lee_(musician) "Shawn Lee (musician)").

## Censorship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Censorship")]

One alteration that Team Soho had to make was the removal of a vehicle and phone box logos which appeared in the initial release of the game. During one of Hammond's missions, a [British Telecom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Telecom "British Telecom") (BT) van is used in a mission in which Hammond must kill the driver and take the van to assassinate a corrupt police officer. BT complained that it "did not want [its] name and livery associated with the violent scenes" in the game, and was worried that it "might incite attacks on [its] engineers". Although the initial release of the game was not recalled, subsequent production was amended to remove the offending details.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-13)

### Ban in Australia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Ban in Australia")]

Originally passed with an [MA 15+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Classification_Board#Restricted "Australian Classification Board") rating for the uncut version on 22 November 2002, it was resubmitted and banned 5 days later due to a scene of detailed torture. A censored version, omitting this scene, was released on 13 December the same year, with the identical rating.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-Game_Power_Australia-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-16)

_The Getaway_ received "average" reviews according to [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-mc-17)_[Maxim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim\_(magazine) "Maxim (magazine)")_ gave the game a score of eight out of ten and wrote: "If the ensuing police brutality doesn't mold you into the model Wheelman, then having to endure those whiny English cop sirens surely will."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-32)_[FHM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FHM "FHM")_ gave it a score of four stars out of five and said: "Not just a little similar to _[GTA III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTA\_III "GTA III")_ in look, feel, and gameplay, it's nonetheless worth sleeping in front of the game store for this one."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-33)

_[The Cincinnati Enquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cincinnati\_Enquirer "The Cincinnati Enquirer")_ gave the game a score of three-and-a-half stars out of five, saying that "the biggest hindrance in _The Getaway_ involves its user interface – or lack thereof – as the development team attempted to make the game look and play out like a movie."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-cincinnati-30)_[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ was very negative of the game, giving it a D and stating: "The level of detail is extraordinary; even the facial expressions are [motion captured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_capture "Motion capture"). But the slickest graphic presentation can't cover for _Getaway_'s flawed script. ... In a game infused with more humor and less pretentious aspirations, these flaws would be more forgivable."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-ew-31)

Sales of _The Getaway_ reached 300,000 copies within two weeks of the game's release.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-ops2sales-34) It had sold over three million copies worldwide by November 2004.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-35) It received a "[Double Platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essentials_(PlayStation) "Essentials (PlayStation)")" sales award from the [Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_and_Leisure_Software_Publishers_Association "Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association") (ELSPA),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-dpelspa-36) indicating sales of at least 600,000 copies in the United Kingdom.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-gamasutrasales-37) By July 2006, _The Getaway_ had sold 1 million copies and earned $36 million in the United States. _[Next Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next\_Generation\_(magazine) "Next Generation (magazine)")_ ranked it as the 53rd highest-selling game launched for the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"), [Xbox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_(console) "Xbox (console)"), or [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") between January 2000 and July 2006 in that country.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-nextgensales2-38)

During the [7th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_Annual_Interactive_Achievement_Awards "7th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards"), the [Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Interactive_Arts_&_Sciences "Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences") nominated _The Getaway_ for "[Outstanding Achievement in Character Performance - Female](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D.I.C.E._Award_for_Outstanding_Achievement_in_Character "D.I.C.E. Award for Outstanding Achievement in Character")" for Anna Edwards' vocal performance as Yasmin.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-39) In a retrospective article from 2014, _[Den of Geek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Den\_of\_Geek "Den of Geek")_ made the game number 23 in their top 50 underappreciated PlayStation 2 games list.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-40) In 2020, _[Push Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Push\_Square "Push Square")_ included the game and its sequel in a list of games they would like to see released on the PlayStation 4.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-41)

### Development of _The Getaway 3_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Development of The Getaway 3")]

_The Getaway 3_ was to be the fourth installment of Sony's _The Getaway_ series for the [PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3") console and the third main installment in the franchise. The title was reported as cancelled on 4 June 2008, along with _[Eight Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight\_Days "Eight Days")_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-SCECancellations-42) In October 2009, the games were reported as not being cancelled, but "on hold".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-News-43) A technical demo featuring [Piccadilly Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piccadilly_Circus "Piccadilly Circus") was demonstrated in May 2005 at [E3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3 "E3"), but this was not directly from the game.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-44) It was confirmed that the game would again be set in London. Information regarding _The Getaway 3_ was released on 7 March 2008 by screenplay writer Katie Ellwood, who affirmed the action title was still in the works. No estimated release date was given, but Ellwood did say that Sony executives were making deals with film companies about the possibility of a future film adaptation of _The Getaway 3_. Nicolas Doucet said: "I would not say they have been abandoned, just put to one side. Much work had been done. The studio just wanted to focus on its strengths, _[EyeToy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EyeToy "EyeToy")_ and _[SingStar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SingStar "SingStar")_. Given the potential of _[EyePet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EyePet "EyePet")_, priorities have been changed, but the other projects aren't dead yet. Ultimately, the decision [to put those games to one side] has benefited everyone".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-45) Richard Bunn, a former developer, had noted the game was cancelled shortly after Phil Harrison was replaced by [Shuhei Yoshida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuhei_Yoshida "Shuhei Yoshida") as president of SCE Worldwide Studios.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-46)

### _Gangs of London_ (2020–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Gangs of London (2020–present)")]

Main article: [Gangs of London (TV series)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangs_of_London_(TV_series) "Gangs of London (TV series)")

[Gareth Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth_Evans_(filmmaker) "Gareth Evans (filmmaker)") and Matt Flannery created a television adaptation of _Gangs of London_ starring [Joe Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Cole_(actor) "Joe Cole (actor)"), [Sope Dirisu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sope_Dirisu "Sope Dirisu"), and an [ensemble cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_cast "Ensemble cast"), which debuted on [Sky Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Atlantic "Sky Atlantic") and [AMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMC_(TV_channel) "AMC (TV channel)") in April 2020,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-48) with Dirisu portraying Elliot Carter / Finch, a character loosely based on _The Getaway_'s Frank Carter, and [Colm Meaney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colm_Meaney "Colm Meaney") portraying Finn Wallace, a character loosely based on _Gangs of London_'s Andy Steele. In an interview with _[Sky News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky\_News "Sky News")_ in April 2020, Evans stated that while initially hired to "make a film franchise" of _Gangs of London_, he had felt like if we were going to do a film franchise, we would have two-thirds of our running time focused purely on our central characters, and then only a third left to explore the side characters that populate that world", and so on deciding that "we wouldn't do justice to the myriad of different diverse cultures and ethnicities that make up the city [I then] pitched it back saying this should be a TV show because you can afford to go off and detour for 10 to 15 minutes and spend time with other characters, and learn about them in more detail."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-49)

### _Ghosts_ (2022)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Ghosts (2022)")]

In December 2022, a _Gangs of London_[graphic novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_novel "Graphic novel"), set between the first and second series of the television adaptation and titled _A Gangs of London Story: Ghosts_, written by [Corin Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corin_Hardy "Corin Hardy") and Rowan Athale and illustrated by Ferenc Nothof, was released digitally to the news aggregator _[Den of Geek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Den\_of\_Geek "Den of Geek")_, ahead of a physical release.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-50)

_**The Getaway**_ is an [action-adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action-adventure "Action-adventure") video game developed by [Team Soho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Soho "Team Soho") and published by [Sony Computer Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Computer_Entertainment "Sony Computer Entertainment") for the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2"). It was released on 11 December 2002. It is inspired by British [gangster films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangster_film "Gangster film") such as _[Get Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get\_Carter "Get Carter")_ (1971) and _[Snatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snatch\_(film) "Snatch (film)")_ (2000).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-SonyUS-2) The game was planned to be released alongside the launch of the PlayStation 2 in 2000, but was delayed by over two years due to the difficulty of recreating large areas of [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") in [high resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_resolution "Image resolution").

_The Getaway_ focuses on two characters: Mark Hammond, an ex-bank robber, and Frank Carter, a police officer in service with the [Flying Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Squad "Flying Squad"). Both plots run parallel and intersect before concluding in the finale of the game. A sequel, _[The Getaway: Black Monday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Getaway:\_Black\_Monday "The Getaway: Black Monday")_, was released in 2004. A spin-off, _[Gangs of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangs\_of\_London\_(video\_game) "Gangs of London (video game)")_, was released in 2006; this spawned the 2020 [television adaptation of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangs_of_London_(TV_series) "Gangs of London (TV series)") and a 2022 graphic novel.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

_The Getaway_ is an [action-adventure game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action-adventure_game "Action-adventure game") played from [third-person view](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-person_view "Third-person view") in which the player controls the two lead characters in an [open world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") as they carry out their missions for game progression. Both of the characters can perform a series of physical tasks such as walking, sprinting, rolling, shooting, and taking cover during a gunfight. Once Mark Hammond's missions are completed, free-roaming is unlocked for his character,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer-3) which allows the player to roam around the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London "City of London") and [Central London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_London "Central London") without mission objectives or time limits. Due to similarities to the _[Grand Theft Auto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Theft\_Auto "Grand Theft Auto")_ series, it is often labeled as a [_Grand Theft Auto_ clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_clone "Grand Theft Auto clone").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-6)

Unlike the _Grand Theft Auto_ series and other similar franchises, the game features a number of real vehicles that were licensed from automobile manufacturers such as [Rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MG_Rover_Group "MG Rover Group"), [Jensen Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jensen_Motors "Jensen Motors"), [Saab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saab_Automobile "Saab Automobile"), [Peugeot Citroën](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peugeot_Citro%C3%ABn "Peugeot Citroën"), [TVR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVR "TVR"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-E3_IGN-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-8)[Fiat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat "Fiat"), and [Lexus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexus "Lexus"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer-3) among others. Firearms are also based on the real world such as [Glock 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glock_17 "Glock 17") pistol, [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") assault rifle, [Remington 870](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remington_870 "Remington 870") pump-action shotgun, and [Heckler & Koch MP5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heckler_&_Koch_MP5 "Heckler & Koch MP5") submachine gun; other weapons include a meat cleaver and crowbar, among others.

A major feature of the game is its approach to being "movie-like" and immersive, which was achieved by excluding features that are present in most games; there is no [HUD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heads-up_display_(video_games) "Heads-up display (video games)") or map system: players driving in a car are guided to a destination by the car's indicators and hazard lights blinking. Running out of ammunition is signaled by the character dropping their weapon, as there isn't a health meter. Player health is regenerated by resting against a wall.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Getaway_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer-3)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Getaway_(video_game)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Plot")]

The game takes place in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") during a single day, and is played through the perspectives of two characters: ex-gangster Mark Hammond and [Metropolitan Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police "Metropolitan Police") officer Frank Carter of the [Flying Squad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Squad "Flying Squad") unit.

_**Doom**_ is a 1993 [first-person shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_shooter "First-person shooter") game developed and published by [id Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Id_Software "Id Software") for [MS-DOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MS-DOS "MS-DOS"). It is the first installment in the [_Doom_ franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(franchise) "Doom (franchise)"). The player [assumes the role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Player_character "Player character") of a [space marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_marine "Space marine"), later unofficially referred to as [Doomguy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomguy "Doomguy"), fighting through hordes of [undead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undead "Undead") humans and invading [demons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demon "Demon"). The game begins on the [moons of Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Mars "Moons of Mars") and finishes in [hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell "Hell"), with the player traversing each level to find its exit or defeat its [final boss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_boss_(video_games) "Final boss (video games)"). It is an early example of [3D graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_graphics "3D graphics") in video games, and has enemies and objects as 2D images, a technique sometimes referred to as [2.5D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2.5D "2.5D") graphics.

_Doom_ was the third major independent release by id Software, after _[Commander Keen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander\_Keen "Commander Keen")_ (1990–1991) and _[Wolfenstein 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfenstein\_3D "Wolfenstein 3D")_ (1992). In May 1992, id started developing a darker game focused on fighting demons with technology, using a new 3D [game engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_engine "Game engine") from the lead programmer, [John Carmack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carmack "John Carmack"). The designer [Tom Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hall "Tom Hall") initially wrote a science fiction plot, but he and most of the story were removed from the project, with the final game featuring an action-heavy design by [John Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Romero "John Romero") and [Sandy Petersen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Petersen "Sandy Petersen"). Id published _Doom_ as a set of three episodes under the [shareware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shareware "Shareware") model, marketing the full game by releasing the first episode free. A retail version with an additional episode was published in 1995 by [GT Interactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GT_Interactive "GT Interactive") as _The Ultimate Doom_.

_Doom_ was a critical and commercial success, earning a reputation as [one of the best](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_games_considered_the_best "List of video games considered the best") and most influential video games of all time. It sold an estimated 3.5 million copies by 1999, and up to 20 million people are estimated to have played it within two years of launch. It has been termed the "father" of first-person shooters and is regarded as one of the most important games in the genre. _Doom_ was included in the first ten "[game canon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_canon "Game canon")" video games selected for preservation by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") in 2007, and its soundtrack was selected for preservation in the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry") in 2026.

The game has been cited by video game historians as shifting the direction and public perception of the medium as a whole, as well as sparking the rise of online games and communities. It led to an array of imitators and [clones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_clone "Video game clone"), as well as [a robust modding scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_modding "Doom modding") and the birth of [speedrunning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedrunning "Speedrunning") as a community. Its high level of [graphic violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_violence "Graphic violence") led to controversy from a range of groups. _Doom_[has been ported](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Doom_ports "List of Doom ports") to a variety of platforms both officially and unofficially and has been followed by several games in the series, including _[Doom II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_II "Doom II")_ (1994), _[Doom 64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_64 "Doom 64")_ (1997), _[Doom 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_3 "Doom 3")_ (2004), _[Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_(2016\_video\_game) "Doom (2016 video game)")_ (2016), _[Doom Eternal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_Eternal "Doom Eternal")_ (2020), and _[Doom: The Dark Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom:\_The\_Dark\_Ages "Doom: The Dark Ages")_ (2025), as well as the films _[Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_(film) "Doom (film)")_ (2005) and _[Doom: Annihilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom:\_Annihilation "Doom: Annihilation")_ (2019).

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Doom_(1993_video_game)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

[![Image 6: A hand holding a chainsaw with enemies standing on a path through green liquid](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/de/Doom_ingame_1.png/250px-Doom_ingame_1.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Doom_ingame_1.png)

Screenshot of the player armed with a chainsaw confronting an undead soldier with a shotgun on a bridge over a chemical waste storage in "Knee-Deep in the Dead"

_Doom_ is a [first-person shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_shooter "First-person shooter") presented with [3D graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_graphics "3D graphics"). While the environment is shown in a 3D perspective, movement is restricted to a [two-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_(mathematics) "Plane (mathematics)") (2D) plane, a technique sometimes referred to as [2.5D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2.5D "2.5D") graphics. The enemies and objects are 2D [sprites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprite_(computer_graphics) "Sprite (computer graphics)") rendered at fixed angles, known as [billboarding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboarding "Billboarding").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-NotTrue3D-4) In the [single-player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-player "Single-player") campaign mode, the player controls an unnamed [space marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_marine "Space marine")—later unofficially termed "[Doomguy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomguy "Doomguy")"—through military bases on the [moons of Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Mars "Moons of Mars") and in [hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell "Hell").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-IGNSEA-5) To finish a [level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_(video_games) "Level (video games)"), the player must traverse through labyrinthine areas to reach a marked exit room. Levels are grouped into named episodes, with the final level of each focusing on a [boss fight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_fight "Boss fight").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-TheGamerGameplay-6)

While traversing the levels, the player must fight a variety of enemies, including [demons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demon "Demon") and [possessed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_possession "Spirit possession")[undead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undead "Undead") humans. Enemies often appear in large groups. The five [difficulty levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Difficulty_level "Difficulty level") adjust the number of enemies and amount of damage they do, with enemies moving and attacking faster than normal on the hardest difficulty setting.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-TheGamerGameplay-6) The monsters have simple behavior: they move toward their opponent if they see or hear them, and attack by biting, clawing, or using magic abilities such as fireballs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-GSAI-7)

The player must manage supplies of ammunition, [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_(game_terminology) "Health (game terminology)"), and armor while traversing the levels. The player can find weapons and ammunition throughout the levels or can collect them from dead enemies, including a [pistol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pistol "Pistol"), a [shotgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shotgun "Shotgun"), a [chainsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainsaw "Chainsaw"), a [plasma rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_rifle "Plasma rifle"), and the [BFG 9000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BFG_9000 "BFG 9000"). The player also encounters pits of [toxic waste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxic_waste "Toxic waste"), ceilings that lower and crush objects, and locked doors requiring a collectable [keycard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keycard "Keycard") or a remote switch.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-MOD124131-8)[Power-ups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power-up "Power-up") include health or armor points, a mapping computer, [partial invisibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invisibility_in_fiction "Invisibility in fiction"), a [radiation suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazmat_suit "Hazmat suit") against toxic waste, invulnerability, or a super-strong melee [berserker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berserker "Berserker") status. [Cheat codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheat_code "Cheat code") allow the player to unlock all weapons, [walk through walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noclip_mode "Noclip mode"), or become invulnerable.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-DoomCheat-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-DoomExtreme-10)

Two [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer "Multiplayer") modes are playable over a network: [cooperative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_video_game "Cooperative video game"), in which two to four players team up to complete the main campaign, and [deathmatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deathmatch_(video_games) "Deathmatch (video games)"), in which two to four players compete to kill the other players' characters as many times as possible.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-DoomVirtualWorlds-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-MOD148153-12) Multiplayer was initially only playable over [local networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_area_network "Local area network"), but a four-player [online multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_multiplayer "Online multiplayer") mode was made available one year after launch through the [DWANGO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DWANGO "DWANGO") service.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-MOD148153-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-MOD182184-13)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Doom_(1993_video_game)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Plot")]

_Doom_ is divided into three episodes, each containing eight main levels: "Knee-Deep in the Dead", "The Shores of Hell", and "Inferno". A fourth episode, "Thy Flesh Consumed", was added in an expanded version, _The Ultimate Doom_, released two years after _Doom_. The campaign contains very few plot elements, with a minimal story presented mostly through the instruction manual and text descriptions between episodes.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-SDF6566-14)

In the future, an unnamed marine is posted to a [dead-end assignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead-end_job "Dead-end job") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_in_fiction "Mars in fiction") after assaulting a superior officer who ordered his unit to fire on civilians. The Union Aerospace Corporation, which operates radioactive waste facilities there, allows the military to conduct secret [teleportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleportation "Teleportation") experiments that turn deadly. A base on [Phobos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobos_(moon) "Phobos (moon)") urgently requests military support, while [Deimos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon) "Deimos (moon)") disappears entirely, and the marine joins a combat force to secure Phobos. He secures the perimeter as ordered while the entire response team is wiped out. With no way off the moon, and armed with only a pistol, he enters the base intent on revenge.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-Manual-15)

In "Knee-Deep in the Dead", the marine fights demons and possessed humans in the military and waste facilities on Phobos. The episode ends with the marine defeating two powerful Barons of Hell guarding a teleporter to the Deimos base. After the battle, the marine passes through the teleporter and is ambushed by a horde of enemies. In "The Shores of Hell", the marine fights through corrupted research facilities on Deimos, culminating in the defeat of a gigantic cyberdemon. From an overlook, he discovers that the moon is floating above hell and rappels down to the surface. In "Inferno", the marine battles through hell itself and destroys a cybernetic spider-demon that masterminded the invasion of the moons. When a portal to Earth opens, the marine steps through to discover that Earth has been invaded. "Thy Flesh Consumed" follows the marine battling the Earth invaders, setting the stage for _[Doom II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_II "Doom II")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom_(1993_video_game)#cite_note-TFCordering-16)
